sentences.t: On 23 September IRDAI released a two-part consultation paper called "Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution".
Its argument is simple.
After the 2023 reforms gave insurers more freedom on how they spend, distribution costs went back up, while the number of people with cover barely moved.
The paper backs that with growth rates.
In a life-insurance sample covering about 92% of corporate-agent premium, new business premium grew 28% between FY23 and FY25 while total distributor pay grew 125% (ET BFSI).
The paper's own line, as quoted by ThePrint, is that "remuneration is growing four to five times faster than the business it is paid on".
In general insurance, premium sourced through brokers grew 37% while commissions grew 173%, and average broker commission went from 8.5% to 17%.
In motor, premium grew about 34% and commissions about 259% (ThePrint).
Two figures describe what the regulator thinks the cost buys.
The first is persistency (the share of policies still active years later).
For life insurance, 61st-month persistency is 48%, against 71% for policies bought online.
The paper reads this as evidence that choices made independently tend to last.
The second is complaints.
General insurance grievances went from 78,347 in FY23 to 1,37,361 in FY25, and nearly 69% of complaints on IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal were linked to claims (ThePrint).
One more number matters because it is about incentives, not averages.
IRDAI says distributor pay is nearly 27% of first-year premium, and rewards and incentives add another 30% to 60% on top of base commission.
So base commission alone understates the real cost (ET BFSI).
That is why the draft counts every form of payment.
The central change is a lower ceiling on expenses of management (EoM, the share of premium an insurer spends on running costs, including commissions).
For life insurers: 15% within two years and 12.5% within five, with cuts starting in FY2027-28.
Insurers already below the benchmark in FY25 would go to 10% within five years.
For general insurers: 25% in two years and 20% in five.

For general insurers, EoM would be measured against gross direct premium income in India, not gross written premium, which removes inward reinsurance and the double counting that comes with it (ET BFSI, ThePrint).
IRDAI would also cut its own fee on insurers from 0.05% to 0.04% of premium, capped at ₹20 crore.
Commission limits would depend on segment, line of business, channel, product complexity and the effort of selling and servicing.
Two adjustments stand out.
Business sourced from towns with populations below 10 lakh would get an extra 10% on the applicable limit, and business from towns below 50,000 people and rural areas an extra 20%.
Distributors in a closed architecture, who can sell only certain insurers' products, would have higher commission opportunities than open-architecture distributors (ET BFSI).
Moneycontrol reports specific caps: first-year commissions of 5% to 20% depending on tenure, health at 15% to 20% for first-time purchases, and renewals and porting at 5% to 10%.
IBAI counts more than 30 caps across products and channels (Hindu BusinessLine).
The exact schedule is in the paper, which I did not read.
All remuneration, direct or indirect, cash or non-cash, would count as commission.
For bank and NBFC staff selling insurance, volume-linked and reward-linked incentives would be banned.
The paper names foreign and domestic trips, luxury gifts, milestone bonuses and contest rewards as examples.
Compulsory bundling of insurance with loans would be prohibited, with specific package offers allowed where there is a demonstrable customer benefit.
Where insurance is offered as additional security, the customer would be told the loan rate with and without it.
Mis-selling would attach to the individual.
The functional identity of the salesperson, PoSP or agent would be tagged to each policy, and mis-selling incidents would become part of a public performance record.
Mis-selling would also trigger commission clawback by the insurer.

Listed practices that could count as mis-selling include presenting a regular-premium product as single premium, selling term cover to people without dependants or outside working age, selling ULIPs to risk-averse or older customers without explaining charges, and selling insurance as a fixed deposit.
Insurers would face mandatory cost audits covering all expenses including non-monetary incentives.
Distributors with insurance revenue above ₹100 crore would need cost audits, and those above ₹50 crore would publicly disclose revenue, expenses, related-party payments and profit after tax.

The draft would replace today's intermediary types with three: Insurance Distribution Entities, Insurance Distribution Persons and Market Infrastructure Institutions, under the principle "same structure, same functions, same norms".
Entry and capital requirements would be lower.
Hospitals could distribute health insurance as entities with lower commission limits, and non-dealer garages could sell motor insurance as associates of insurers.
Market Infrastructure Institutions are digital, not-for-profit marketplaces.
Bima Sugam is named as one, and IRDAI expects it to be running with a wide range of products in four to six months.
Starting one would need at least 11 insurers with no significant holder (ET BFSI).
The stated aim is a model where "insurance is also purchased", not only sold.
Reading several outlets side by side shows gaps that only the paper can settle.
The EoM base.
ET BFSI says life insurers would go to 15% "of premium".
The Hindu says 15% "of gross direct premium income", from a present level of 30% to 35%.
These are different yardsticks, and I do not know which is right.
Motor commissions.
ET BFSI gives an average of about 24% across a range of 13% to 50%.
ThePrint says motor commissions nearly tripled from about 9% to 25%.
These can both be true if one is a level and the other a change, but the outlets do not say so.
The size of the cut.
CNBC-TV18 quotes Swami Saran Sharma of Helios Global Solutions saying the proposal cuts commissions by about 10%.
The Moneycontrol caps look like cuts of very different sizes by product.
I cannot reconcile the two without the paper.
The deadline.
Feedback closes on 25 October.
IBAI asked on 6 October for the end of December.
IRDAI has not, in anything I read, agreed.
A Moneycontrol interview with chairman Ajay Seth is headlined "IRDAI rules out glide path for commission caps", but it is paywalled and I could not read it.

Monika Halan, a financial educator, told India Today the proposal puts the policyholder at the centre for the first time and that removing caps in 2023 produced "a free-for-all", with commissions, costs, mis-selling complaints and unpaid claims all rising.
She thinks two and five years are too slow and says the cap should apply within six months.

The India Today piece also describes two mis-selling cases, a retired Kolkata couple who paid about ₹12 lakh for two policies sold by a bank assistant manager, and a Mumbai man told he needed insurance to get a ₹40 lakh loan (India Today).
Those are individual accounts in a news story, not data.
Mahavir Chopra of insurtech Beshak does not dispute that mis-selling and excess commission exist.
His objection is that a common cap treats a distributor who explains exclusions and helps with claims the same as one who only processes a transaction.
He suggests grading pay by product complexity and distributor capability, with part of it tied to persistency, complaints and satisfaction.

Thomas Devasia, a former IRDAI member for non-life, told CNBC-TV18 that hard caps are regressive because tightening the EoM framework would have been enough, and that the problem was enforcement of the 2023 rules (CNBC-TV18).
IBAI, which represents brokers and so has a direct interest, argues four things.
First, the 2023 framework has a scheduled review in 2028, and the draft reverses it "without a regulatory impact assessment".
Second, the paper has no mechanism to make sure savings reach policyholders as lower premiums, so, it says, savings would move from distributors' and insurers' employees to insurers' owners.
Third, an "untested" framework that does not exist elsewhere in the world needs wider consultation.

Fourth, jobs: it estimates at least 10 lakh livelihoods at risk over five years, which it itself calls a preliminary estimate, against a total of more than 83 lakh distribution professionals by IRDAI's data.
IBAI also supports parts of the draft: the ban on compulsory loan bundling, stronger suitability checks, and clawbacks for proven mis-selling (CNBC-TV18, Hindu BusinessLine).
One point nobody in the coverage rebuts directly: IBAI's claim that savings would not reach customers.
IRDAI's stated aim is to expand the risk pool and improve policyholder returns, but the reports I read do not show a mechanism either way.
From here, my analysisEverything above is reported.
This section is my reading of those reports.
It is a set of questions and plausible effects, not findings.
Indraneel Chatterjee, co-founder of InsuranceDekho, gave Moneycontrol two worked examples.
A 5% commission on an own-damage premium of ₹800 leaves ₹40 at the entity level, before PoSP splits.
A PoSP who sells three or four policies a month with combined premium of about ₹20,000 would, at a 4% net rate after broker retention, earn about ₹800 a month.
The sums check out (5% of ₹800 is ₹40, and 4% of ₹20,000 is ₹800).
The inputs are his assumptions, and he runs an affected business.
The point stands as an illustration: on low-ticket products, a flat percentage leaves almost nothing for field effort.
The draft's 10% and 20% allowances for small towns and rural areas look like a partial answer to this, but I have not seen anyone quantify them.

IIFL Capital, quoted by Business Standard, puts the banking system's bancassurance income pool at about $2.2 billion, around 10% of bank fee income, close to 3% of profit after tax and about 6 basis points of return on assets.
Analysts therefore see a limited profit impact.
They expect banks to reconsider which products they push in branches, favouring higher-commission ones and offsetting lower payouts with volume.
The loan-bundling ban and the staff-incentive ban hit the bank channel in a different way, because they change how branch staff are paid and what they can attach to a loan (Business Standard).
A lower EoM ceiling forces insurers to find savings somewhere.
Commissions are the largest controllable item, which is why the two parts of the draft go together.
The Business Standard report adds that insurers could steer business to group companies where the economics are easier to manage.
The Hindu notes the timing, six months after FDI in insurance was raised to 100%, and asks whether the transition treats new and established insurers differently.
That question is the Hindu's, not a finding.
Moneycontrol reports PB Fintech fell 15% and Turtlemint 20% after the paper was released, and ThePrint says insurance stocks came under sharp selling.
One day's move is not a verdict.
The draft cuts two ways for this group.
Lower commissions squeeze margins, while the push towards digital and pull-based buying through Bima Sugam could bring in new competitors, or in IRDAI's framing, remove layers.
Which effect dominates depends on the final caps, which are not yet written.
The draft is two arguments in one document.
One is about cost, and the evidence IRDAI gives on pay outrunning premium is strong.
The other is about what the cost buys, and nobody has shown yet how a cap turns into better persistency or fewer claim disputes.
For your own work, three questions would sharpen your view before the deadline.
What share of your distribution is low-ticket, where a flat cap bites hardest?
What evidence of advice and servicing effort do you currently keep per policy, given the paper ties pay to effort?
And how much of your revenue depends on renewal commission, given the reported 5% to 10% renewal and porting caps in health?
